title: PKCE Flow
description: Secure public client authentication using Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) with OAuth2.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **PKCE Flow**. Secure public client authentication using Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) with OAuth2. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of PKCE Flow and be confident in applying it to your projects.
Why PKCE Exists

In a plain Authorization Code flow, the authorization code is passed through the browser's front channel. An attacker who can intercept the code (via a malicious app registering a custom URL scheme, network eavesdropping, or log injection) can exchange it for tokens. PKCE eliminates this risk: the client generates a random secret (code_verifier) and its transformation (code_challenge) upfront. The authorization server stores the challenge with the code. When the client exchanges the code, it must present the original verifier, which only the legitimate client possesses.

items: code_verifier: A high-entropy random string generated by the client.
code_challenge: BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(code_verifier)) — the transformed value sent to the authorization server.
code_challenge_method: S256 is the only acceptable method. Avoid plain (plaintext) at all costs.
transform: The mathematical operation used to derive the challenge (SHA256 with S256).

data.caption: PKCE Authorization Code Flow with code verifier and challenge
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client
    participant AuthServer
    participant API
    Client->>Client: Generate code_verifier
    Client->>Client: Generate code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))
    Client->>AuthServer: Redirect with code_challenge, method=S256
    AuthServer->>User: Login & Consent
    User->>AuthServer: Submit credentials
    AuthServer->>Client: Redirect with authorization code
    Client->>AuthServer: POST code + code_verifier to token endpoint
    AuthServer->>AuthServer: Verify SHA256(code_verifier) == code_challenge
    AuthServer->>Client: access_token + refresh_token + id_token
    Client->>API: Request with access_token
    API->>Client: Protected resource

data.title: Never use plain PKCE method
data.text: If code_challenge_method is set to 'plain', the challenge is just the raw verifier in plaintext. An attacker who intercepts the challenge can use it directly as the verifier. Always use S256 (SHA-256 hashing). Most modern authorization servers reject plain challenges from non-legacy clients.

data.text: Step by Step: PKCE in Four Phases

items: At the start of the login flow, generate a code_verifier (random string) and compute code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)). Store verifier locally and pass only the challenge.
Send the user to the authorization endpoint with code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 instead of (or in addition to) client_id.
After the user authenticates, redirect back with the authorization code. The authorization server will have stored the code_challenge alongside the code.
POST the authorization code AND the original code_verifier to the token endpoint. The server runs SHA256(code_verifier) and compares it to the stored code_challenge. If they match, it issues tokens.

rows: Verifier is hashed before sending; intercepted codes are useless.
Challenge equals the verifier; defeating the protection.

data.title: Where to store the code_verifier
data.text: In a single-page app, store the verifier in memory (not localStorage) to reduce XSS exposure. In a mobile app, use the platform's secure keychain. The verifier must survive the redirect round-trip but should be single-use and short-lived.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: PKCE extends Authorization Code flow for public clients that cannot store a secret
code_verifier is a random secret; code_challenge is its SHA-256 hash
The verifier proves the token exchange request is from the same client that started the flow
Store the verifier in memory or a secure keychain, tied to the session
PKCE is required for mobile apps and strongly recommended for all SPAs
data.takeaway: PKCE turns an interceptable authorization code into a useless string without the matching verifier, closing the main gap in the Authorization Code flow for public clients.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid
Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **PKCE Flow**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of PKCE Flow when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations
Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **PKCE Flow**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **PKCE Flow**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
